title: Miserable Comforters and a Witness in Heaven
summary: Job calls his friends miserable comforters and says that if their places were reversed he would strengthen them instead of attacking them. He describes God as an enemy who has torn him, seized him by the neck, and set him up as a target for archers, while men strike his cheeks. Yet, protesting that his hands are free of violence, he declares that even now he has a witness in heaven who will plead his case with God.
story: Eliphaz has just opened the second round of the debate with a sharp rebuke and a long portrait of the wicked man's ruin (chapter 15). Job's reply runs through chapters 16 and 17. In chapter 16 his sense of being attacked by God reaches its most violent images in the book so far. At the same time, and in the same speech, his hope rises higher. In chapter 9 he lamented that there was no mediator between him and God. Here he says that there is a witness in heaven. The thread of an advocate or redeemer that began with that lament will climb to its peak in chapter 19, where Job declares that his Redeemer lives.
historical:
The chapter draws on the language of ancient law and ancient warfare. Legal ideas run through its opening and close. In verse 8 Job's own wasted body becomes a witness testifying against him, since in the friends' logic his suffering proves guilt. In verse 19 he looks for a witness on his side, and in verse 21 for someone to argue his case with God as one person argues with a neighbor. The idea that a murdered person's blood cries out from the ground for justice (verse 18) goes back to the story of Cain and Abel (Genesis 4:10), and Israel's law treated innocent blood as a pollution that had to be answered (Numbers 35:33).

The military images in verses 12-14 reflect the warfare of the ancient Near East. Archers were a central part of armies, and attackers besieged walled cities by opening a breach and pouring through it. Job pictures himself first as a man seized by the neck, then as a target surrounded by archers, and finally as a city whose walls are broken open breach after breach.
cultural:
Job's actions of mourning in verses 15-16 were standard in his world. Sackcloth was coarse cloth, usually of goat hair, worn next to the skin in grief or repentance. Job has sewn it on, as if it had become a permanent part of him. The horn was a symbol of strength and dignity, drawn from the horns of wild oxen; to bury one's horn in the dust was to have one's honor brought to nothing. Shaking the head at someone (verse 4) and striking the cheek (verse 10) were public gestures of contempt, the second an especially deep insult in a culture where honor was carried in the face.

The comforter was a recognized role in ancient mourning. Friends came to sit with the grieving, share their sorrow, and speak words that strengthened them. Job's friends began well by sitting silently for seven days (2:13). In verse 5 Job describes what they should have done: encourage with the mouth and bring relief with the lips.
literary: The chapter moves from friends to God and back to hope. Verses 1-6 rebuke the friends as miserable comforters. Verses 7-14 describe God's assault in a rush of violent images: a wild beast tearing and gnashing its teeth, an attacker who seizes by the neck, a commander of archers, a warrior breaking through walls. Some lines in verses 7-9 shift between he and you, speaking about God and to him, a sign of Job's turmoil. Verses 15-17 describe Job's mourning and assert his innocence. Verses 18-22 turn upward: an appeal to the earth not to cover his blood, and a confession that his witness is in heaven. The move from God as attacker in verses 9-14 to God (or someone with God) as witness in verse 19 is the chapter's great paradox. Job appeals to God against God.

outline.t: God's assault: torn, seized, and shot at
Sackcloth, tears, and a clean conscience

doctrines.note: Job experiences God as his attacker, and the Bible records that experience without softening it. Faith here is not the absence of that experience but the refusal to let it be the last word.

At the lowest point of the chapter Job declares that his witness is in heaven. He clings to a hope of vindication beyond anything he can see, appealing to God even while he feels God's hand against him.
Job says his prayer is pure (verse 17) and that his eyes pour out tears to God (verse 20). Even his complaint is directed toward God, and he longs for someone to plead his case there.

words.note: Sahed, witness, a word borrowed from Aramaic that appears only here in the Hebrew Bible. The related Aramaic phrase Jegar-sahadutha, heap of witness, appears in Genesis 31:47. In verse 19 it stands in parallel with the ordinary Hebrew word for witness: Job has someone on high who will testify for him.

Ed, witness, one who testifies in a legal case. In verse 8 Job's wasted body is a witness against him; in verse 19 he has a witness in heaven on his side. The word ties the chapter's despair and its hope together.
Yakach, to argue or decide a case. In verse 21 it expresses Job's longing that someone would plead with God for a man as one pleads for a neighbor. It is the same root that gave the arbiter of 9:33.
Dam, blood. When Job cries to the earth not to cover his blood (verse 18), he draws on the belief, first seen with Abel in Genesis 4:10, that innocent blood cries out to God until justice is done.

christ: The chapter holds two threads that the New Testament ties to Christ, both thematic rather than predictive. The first is the heavenly witness and advocate. John writes that if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1), and Hebrews says Christ always lives to intercede for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). The second is the innocent sufferer struck on the cheek. Job says men strike his cheeks with contempt (verse 10); the Gospels record that Jesus was struck and spat upon before his crucifixion (Matthew 26:67). Hebrews also contrasts Abel's blood, which cried for justice, with the blood of Jesus, which speaks a better word (Hebrews 12:24). Job longs for a witness and an advocate in heaven; the New Testament presents Jesus as both.

hard.q: Who is the witness in heaven in verse 19?
hard.a: Job has just described God as his attacker, yet he says, “Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high.” Interpreters identify this witness in three main ways. Many think it is God himself: Job appeals from the God who seems to be against him to the God he trusts is ultimately just, a kind of appeal from God to God. Others think Job imagines a heavenly figure distinct from God, such as an angelic intercessor (Eliphaz mentioned holy ones in 5:1, and Elihu will speak of a mediating angel in 33:23). A third view takes the witness to be Job's own cry or prayer, rising to heaven and testifying for him, which fits verse 18 and the tears of verse 20. Christians have often read the verse in light of Christ as advocate, while recognizing that Job could not have had Jesus in mind. The text leaves the identity open, and its force lies in Job's confidence that someone in heaven is on his side.

questions: Job tells his friends what he would have done in their place: encourage and bring relief. What does good comfort sound like when you are the one speaking?
Job feels God is against him and yet says his witness is in heaven. How can someone hold both of those at the same time?
What difference does it make to you that Christians believe they have an advocate with the Father?
